$comment: Spec 120 §3.4-§3.4b — the INTERPRETATION file for link_massing, capped at 12 prose
entries. Checks are uncapped; prose is capped, because the cheapest way to keep
knowledge is to make it measurable. Every entry carries measured{value, date, query}
so it can be re-executed rather than believed, and a `decisions` entry is exempt only
because a ruling is not a measurement.
Everything in here lived ONLY as a source comment before this conversion, and would
have been deleted with the 740 lines it was attached to.

read_this_way.note: The predicate is BUILDING-CENTROID-IN-PARCEL, and the direction is the whole point. A detached house covers roughly a third of its lot, so the LOT's centroid usually lands in the yard rather than inside the house — the pre-flip predicate (parcel centroid inside building polygon) therefore missed most single-family parcels. The building's centre of mass, by contrast, is always inside the building and almost always on the lot that owns it. Reading a low link rate on this step means the join broke, not that the city is sparsely built.

measured.value: parcel coverage 58% before the flip, 99.71% after
measured.query: SELECT round(100.0 * count(DISTINCT pb.parcel_id) / (SELECT count(*) FROM parcels WHERE centroid_lat IS NOT NULL AND centroid_lng IS NOT NULL), 2) FROM parcel_buildings pb

read_this_way.note: The link rate reported in the audit table is CUMULATIVE, not run-scoped, and that is deliberate rather than lazy. In incremental mode the eligible set is exactly the parcels that have never linked — a pool that is permanently unmatchable, because they were already offered every footprint within the fallback radius and matched none — so a run-scoped rate reads 0% on a perfectly healthy run and would fire the floor every time. The row answers 'what fraction of the city is linked', which is the question a consumer actually has.

measured.value: run-scoped rate 0% vs cumulative 99.71% on the same run
measured.query: SELECT records_meta->'audit_table'->'rows' FROM pipeline_runs WHERE pipeline LIKE '%link_massing' AND status='completed' ORDER BY completed_at DESC LIMIT 1

read_this_way.note: The nearest fallback's bbox prefilter converts metres to degrees by dividing by 78000 — metres per degree of longitude at Toronto's latitude. It OVER-covers east-west on purpose: the prefilter must be a superset of the true cut, and the exact cut is the geography ST_DWithin that follows. Changing 78000 changes what '50 metres' costs to find, never how much of it is accepted. Dropping the prefilter entirely is the failure tasks/lessons.md records: the geography distance then runs a nested loop over every footprint in the table, per batch.

known_normal.note: Every incremental run processes the SAME 1,395 parcels, matches none of them, writes nothing, and reports PASS. That is the steady state, not a stall: the incremental filter selects parcels with no link at all, so it re-walks the permanently-unmatchable tail forever. The founding comment on the downstream massing_zero_link_ghost guard claims a 'measured day-one value 0' for this tail; no cloud observation supports it and both recorded cloud rows read 1395, confirmed locally here. review_followups.md files the correction; do not treat 1,395 as a regression.

measured.query: SELECT count(*) FROM parcels p WHERE p.centroid_lat IS NOT NULL AND p.centroid_lng IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM parcel_buildings pb WHERE pb.parcel_id = p.id)

known_normal.note: A run that writes ZERO rows while reporting hundreds of matches is correct, not broken. The upsert is guarded on the four value columns, so re-offering an identical link is a genuine no-op — that is what makes the step re-runnable. The row to read for 'did anything change' is parcel_buildings_written; the row to read for 'did the join work' is match_centroid_in_parcel.

measured.query: SELECT started_at, records_total, records_new, records_updated FROM pipeline_runs WHERE pipeline LIKE '%link_massing' AND status='completed' ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 5

known_bad.note: 21.3% of linked parcels are linked ONLY by the nearest fallback at the lower confidence, and 49.06% of THOSE carry a footprint larger than their own lot — a physical impossibility that marks a mislink. The links are produced here, shipped, and NULLed one chain-step later by enrich-parcels' footprint_exceeds_lot guard. Since peel 8b the population is COUNTED at the link (`nearest_footprint_gt_lot_count`, by match_type) instead of only downstream; it is INFO and not gated, because this is a data-quality class rather than staleness — a forced full relink moves none of it, and a WARN would redden every production run for a condition the conversion did not create. ⚠️ READ THE TREND, NOT THE LEVEL: the LM-D13 tiebreak itself moved this from 48,646 to 50,790 (+2,144) because resolving a distance tie in favour of the LARGER footprint puts more primaries above their lot line. That is a declared consequence of the rule, not a regression, and it is the reason the counter exists.

measured.value: 103,530 nearest-only parcels; 50,790 of them footprint > lot (48,646 before the tiebreak); 13,347 of 381,605 centroid_in_parcel primaries
measured.query: SELECT pb.match_type, count(*) FILTER (WHERE bf.footprint_area_sqm > p.lot_size_sqm) AS gt_lot, count(*) AS n FROM parcel_buildings pb JOIN parcels p ON p.id=pb.parcel_id JOIN building_footprints bf ON bf.id=pb.building_id WHERE pb.is_primary GROUP BY 1

known_bad.note: LM-D13 — the nearest fallback's SELECTION RULE, and why it is a rule rather than an accident. `DISTINCT ON (p.id)` keeps the FIRST row of the sort, so the ORDER BY *is* the answer to 'which building does this parcel get'. With distance alone an equidistant pair has no ordering between its members and the winner was whatever the plan emitted first: 18,252 of the 103,530 nearest links could flip between two otherwise identical full relinks, 17,566 of them tied at distance 0 (a footprint overlapping the lot with its centroid outside it). Since peel 8b the order is `p.id, ST_Distance(...) ASC, bf.footprint_area_sqm DESC, bf.id ASC` — distance FIRST, because a tiebreak that re-ranks is not a tiebreak; then the fence-5bb31faf order, so the fallback answers the question the same way the centroid pass has always answered it: the largest footprint wins, the lowest building_id settles the rest. The area term is what makes the choice MEAN something (on a semi or a shared driveway the larger overlapping structure is the one the cost model is asking about); bf.id is the total-order backstop.

measured.value: two forced FULL relinks now hash-EQUAL; before the tiebreak they read a0023203 vs 0d2ea577 with all 8 invariants identical
measured.query: SELECT count(*) FROM parcel_buildings WHERE match_type = 'nearest'

blind_spots.what: CLOSED AT PEEL 8b, kept as the record of what was invisible: nothing counted a footprint-exceeds-lot link AT THE LINK. The condition was caught one chain-step downstream by enrich-parcels, which NULLs the whole existing-structure block for the affected parcel, so the bad links were produced, shipped and silently discarded while this step's audit table read PASS throughout. `nearest_footprint_gt_lot_count` now reports it by match_type on every run. What is still open is the CONSEQUENCE, not the count: the 58,050 downstream flags remain, and the sanity-harness gap below is a separate WF3.

measured.value: 58,050 parcels flagged footprint_exceeds_lot downstream; 50,790 + 13,347 now counted here
measured.query: SELECT count(*) FROM parcels WHERE existing_data_quality_flag = 'footprint_exceeds_lot'

blind_spots.what: The parcel sanity harness has ZERO rules over parcel_buildings itself — its four massing rules all fire on the DERIVED parcel columns, so a mislink is caught only after it has become a cost. parcel-field-dump.js likewise shows no link-level field (match_type / confidence / is_primary / footprints-per-parcel), so an eyeball on a suspicious parcel cannot see how it was linked. Filed as a separate WF3.

suspicious_if.signal: parcel_buildings_written is large on a run whose match counts did not move. The guard makes an unchanged link a no-op, so writes without matches means something is changing the four guarded value columns — most plausibly a confidence or threshold edit, or the run clock having reached the change guard.

measured.value: 0 rows written on every run since 2026-07-08
measured.query: SELECT started_at, records_updated FROM pipeline_runs WHERE pipeline LIKE '%link_massing' AND status='completed' ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 10

decisions.note: A-8 OVERRIDE — the JS fallback path is RETIRED, not pinned. It was a complete second implementation of this step's contract (in-memory grid, haversine, Mercator auto-detect, turf point-in-polygon, batch size 500, its own confidence literals, and NO is_primary clear before the upsert) that has never executed: every recorded run reports the PostGIS branch. Retiring it removes the §1.6 silent swallow it carried — an invalid geometry in the point-in-polygon test was caught, logged and the parcel silently reclassified as no-match with no counter — and replaces the branch with a fail-loud guards.requires precondition on the extension.

fences.const: the is_primary clear precedes the upsert, and the primary sort is area DESC then building_id ASC
fences.incident: PostGIS argument order + deterministic primary assignment + the partial unique index. Without the clear, a parcel whose largest building changes violates idx_parcel_buildings_one_primary the moment the new primary is upserted while the old one is still flagged; without the building_id tiebreak in the sort, two equal-area buildings take turns being primary between runs. B-8.

fences.const: the upsert's IS DISTINCT FROM guard names exactly is_primary/structure_type/match_type/confidence and NEVER linked_at
fences.incident: Before this guard the upsert re-stamped every row it touched. linked_at is in the SET list but excluded from the guard because it is the run clock: including it — or writing guard_columns "all_declared", which expands over it — makes every one of 520,492 rows DISTINCT on every run, and enrich-parcels re-scopes on pb.linked_at so the next enrich run goes from 1,395 parcels to 485,135. D-5.

fences.const: the full-mode retraction is ONE statement, before the loop, scoped identically to the parcels being re-evaluated
fences.value: retract "all" + retract_when "full_only" + write_discipline.scope = the centroid base filter
fences.incident: The predicate flip left GHOST LINKS: rows that matched under the old parcel-centroid-in-building test and not under the new one. The cleanup must retract exactly the set the run rebuilds — a wider scope empties the junction for parcels this run never revisits, and an ungated one would retract 520,492 rows on an incremental run that rebuilds only the 1,395-parcel tail. B-7.

fences.const: the nearest cap comes from massing_nearest_max_distance_m, and the ST_Expand bbox prefilter precedes the geography ST_DWithin
fences.value: config.massing_nearest_max_distance_m -> $3, and its /78000 degree span -> $2 in ST_Expand
fences.incident: The three massing heuristics were externalized out of the code. Re-literalising the cap makes it an invisible knob again; dropping or reordering the prefilter makes the geography distance a nested loop over every footprint, per batch, which is the incident tasks/lessons.md records. B-10.

fences.const: the full relink is GATED on a real change, not on the --full argument alone
fences.value: staleness.mode_select "tri_state": full iff forced, or (--full permitted AND a code/corpus signal moved)
fences.incident: The --full chain_arg served a one-time ghost-link cleanup; leaving it always-on cost ~21.9 minutes on every quarterly sources run even when nothing had changed. The gate needs BOTH signals: a pure data gate would have silently skipped the predicate flip itself, leaving ghost links.

fences.const: linked_at is written on INSERT so a first-time link is never NULL
fences.value: columns[].source "run_at" on linked_at, stamped by the runner from one DB-clock capture
fences.incident: First-time links landed with a NULL linked_at, which made the downstream watermark comparison silently skip them forever. Spec 47 §6.1. The runner now stamps it from a single getDbTimestamp per run, so two batches cannot straddle a second either (B-11).

fences.const: the nearest fallback resolves a distance tie by a declared rule: ORDER BY p.id, ST_Distance(...) ASC, bf.footprint_area_sqm DESC, bf.id ASC
fences.value: distance first (the tiebreak breaks ties, it does not re-rank), then the fence-5bb31faf order: largest footprint wins, lowest building_id settles the remainder. Locked both directions as text in the lock_test (F5: every reversion shape — a dropped term, a flipped direction, a term hoisted above the distance, no ORDER BY at all) and behaviourally in src/tests/steps/link_massing/nearest-determinism.test.ts, which runs the production statement 40 times over a randomly ordered scan of a 0-distance tie and asserts one winner with the rule and BOTH winners without it
fences.incident: LM-D13, discovered by measurement rather than by a fix( commit — the Severity: footer census on this file is 0 and the construct was never wrong enough to be reported. `9ff540ec` is the commit that PINNED it verbatim and declared it (the conversion diff had to move zero rows); peel 8b is where the rule landed. Before it the ORDER BY carried distance alone, so DISTINCT ON kept whichever equidistant row the plan emitted first: 18,252 of 103,530 nearest links could flip between two identical full relinks (17,566 tied at distance 0), and two forced relinks hashed a0023203 vs 0d2ea577 with every invariant equal. Dropping either term, flipping its direction, or hoisting it above ST_Distance all reintroduce it.

review_notes.note: Read the two write targets as ONE ordered pair, never independently: the primary clear is only correct because the upsert follows it in the same transaction, and the upsert is only safe because the clear preceded it. A review that asks 'why is this UPDATE unguarded' in isolation gets the wrong answer.

measured.value: 2 declared write targets, executed in declaration order
